planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed. This heat-loving African eggplant has no frost tolerance.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; Round Green African Eggplant produces round, green-and-white striped fruit about 4 inches across, maturing in roughly 90 days. The fruit is eaten boiled, fried, or simmered into sauces, often as a meat substitute in West African cooking. Like other Solanum aethiopicum types it thrives in heat and needs a full warm season to produce a good crop, performing especially well in hot Gulf Coast summers.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed. This dual-purpose type yields leaves at 30 days and fruit at 60 days.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; Nigerian Garden Egg is a dual-purpose African eggplant known as Efo Igbo or Ganyen Gauta, grown both for its leaves, harvestable in about 30 days for garden egg leaf soup and dishes like abacha, and its fruit, ready around 60 days. Plants reach 3-5 feet, thriving in heat with no frost tolerance. Harvest leaves regularly to encourage continued production through the warm season.

scientific_name: Solanum aethiopicum var. gilo 'Striped Garden Egg'

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Striped Garden Egg is a Gilo-type African eggplant producing 3-inch, lightly bitter striped fruit on tall 4-5 foot plants, traditionally harvested green-and-white and eaten raw, boiled, sautéed, or added to soup. The young leaves are also cooked into stews, giving the plant dual culinary use. Give it the full warm season it needs to mature, performing especially well in long, hot Gulf Coast summers.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Nya Nya Chungu is a Congolese African eggplant maturing in about 60 days from transplant, its fruit traditionally peeled and halved for cooking with meat, fish, and greens, or salted and eaten raw. It is a heat-loving warm-season annual with no frost tolerance, needing full sun and a long growing season for best production. This cultivar carries a folk reputation among growers for traditional blood-sugar-management use, though that claim is anecdotal rather than clinically established.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Gbogname is grown mainly for its leaves rather than fruit.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Gbogname is an ancient Togolese landrace of gboma eggplant, grown primarily as a leafy green for its densely nutritious, regularly harvestable leaves, with its bitter yellow fruit of secondary culinary interest. It is treated as a tropical perennial in frost-free climates or a warm-season annual elsewhere, reaching 2-4 feet. Harvest leaves continually through the growing season for the best yield, much like harvesting a cut-and-come-again green.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil reaches about 65°F after last frost; A.L. Teff is an Ethiopian grain selection, distinct from the American forage-grass teff cultivars already grown for hay.

directions: Direct sow into warm soil in full sun once the soil reaches roughly 65°F; A.L. Teff is an Ethiopian grain selection of teff, distinct from the American forage-grass breeding lines already in cultivation, grown specifically for its tiny, gluten-free grain used to mill injera flour. It is a fast-growing warm-season annual with no frost tolerance, reaching full maturity and seed set in 90-120 days. Harvest when seed heads turn golden-brown and thresh by hand or with a fine screen, since the grain is extremely small.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into warm, fertile soil in full sun; Madiira 1 was bred specifically as a leafy vegetable type, not for grain or ornamental use.

directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in full sun; Madiira 1 was released in 2011 by Horti-Tengeru and the World Vegetable Center in Tanzania as a leafy vegetable amaranth, also known regionally as Ex-Zim or KK Mrambi, selected for leaves that stay green longer and for preferred taste and cooking quality compared to common landraces. It carries higher iron, calcium, and fiber content than typical amaranth greens, making it a nutritionally valuable warm-season crop. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips repeatedly through the season as a cut-and-come-again potherb.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into warm, fertile soil in full sun; Madiira 2 is the companion release to Madiira 1, with a similarly improved nutritional profile.

directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in full sun; Madiira 2 is a companion release to Madiira 1 from the same Tanzania-based World Vegetable Center breeding program, also known regionally as AM38 or KK Livokoyi, offering a similarly improved iron, calcium, and fiber content along with stable leaf yield through the growing season. It is grown the same way as Madiira 1, as a cut-and-come-again leafy green in East African home gardens and increasingly elsewhere. Harvest young leaves repeatedly for the best quality and continued production.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into average soil in full sun; Woolflower is more often foraged as a semi-wild potherb than sold as a formal named cultivar.

directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Woolflower is a genuine African potherb, distinct from the already-grown Celosia argentea, growing wild as a savanna weed across tropical Africa and widely harvested young for its leaves and stems, which are boiled like cabbage in a dish sometimes called torchata. It is an annual reaching about 3 feet, with no frost tolerance, and is more commonly foraged than sold as a formal named retail cultivar, so treat it as a species-level addition for an African ethnobotanical garden rather than a branded variety.
